paragraphs.heading: What an electron is
paragraphs.text: An electron is a subatomic particle with an electric charge of negative one elementary charge. It is an elementary particle found in the matter that makes up the universe. Every atom contains electrons along with protons and neutrons, but electrons are far lighter: an electron has about 1/1836 the mass of a proton. In an atom, an electron's matter wave spreads through atomic orbitals around the positively charged nucleus.

paragraphs.heading: Electrons and chemistry
paragraphs.text: How an atom's electrons are arranged, and their energy levels, set the atom's chemical properties. Some electrons are bound to the nucleus more tightly than others. The outermost ones, called valence electrons, are the most loosely bound, and they form the chemical bonds that build molecules and crystals. They also make every kind of chemical reaction possible by being passed or shared between atoms, while the inner electron shells make up the atomic core.

paragraphs.heading: Electricity and electronics
paragraphs.text: Electrons explain a great deal of physics. In metals the outermost electrons are free to move around, which accounts for how well metals conduct electricity and heat. In semiconductors, the number of mobile charge carriers can be finely adjusted, and that control is the basis of modern electronics. Electrons can also exist as free particles: in a vacuum, beams of them can be sped up and focused for cathode ray tubes, electron microscopes, electron beam welding and particle accelerators.

paragraphs.heading: Particle and wave
paragraphs.text: Electrons belong to the lepton family, particles that do not feel the strong nuclear force. They have no known smaller parts, so they are generally treated as elementary particles. Like all elementary particles, they act both as particles and as waves: they can collide with other particles, and they can also be diffracted the way light is. Their wave side is easier to see in experiments than that of protons or neutrons, because an electron's lower mass gives it a longer wavelength at a given energy. Being fermions, no two electrons can share the same quantum state, a rule called the Pauli exclusion principle.

paragraphs.heading: Beta particles and positrons
paragraphs.text: Electrons also play a part in nuclear reactions, for example nucleosynthesis inside stars; in that role they are called beta particles. New electrons are made when radioactive isotopes undergo beta decay, and in high-energy collisions, for example when cosmic rays enter the atmosphere. The electron's antiparticle is the positron, identical in every way except that its charge has the opposite sign. When an electron and a positron collide, both can be annihilated, leaving gamma ray photons.

paragraphs.heading: Named after amber
paragraphs.text: The ancient Greeks saw that amber rubbed with fur would attract small objects, which, together with lightning, is among humanity's earliest recorded experiences of electricity. In 1600 the English scientist William Gilbert, writing in his treatise De Magnete, invented the Neo-Latin word electrica for substances that, like amber, attract small objects after being rubbed. The words electric and electricity come from the Latin ēlectrum, which came from the Greek word for amber, ēlektron.

paragraphs.heading: One fluid or two
paragraphs.text: In the early 1700s, the French chemist Charles François du Fay found that a charged gold leaf pushed away by glass rubbed with silk was drawn toward amber rubbed with wool. From experiments like this he concluded that electricity was two fluids, a vitreous one and a resinous one, which neutralize each other when combined. Later Benjamin Franklin proposed instead that electricity was a single fluid, showing either an excess (+) or a deficit (−).
